{{short description|Unique circle centered at a given triangle's orthocenter}}
[[File:Polar circle2.svg|thumb|upright=1.25|
{{legend-line|solid #4169E1|Reference triangle {{math|△''ABC''}}}}
{{legend-line|solid #82c458|[[Altitude (triangle)|Altitudes]] (concur at [[orthocenter]] {{mvar|H}}; intersect [[extended side]]s of {{math|△''ABC''}} at {{mvar|D, E, F}})}}

]]

In [[geometry]], the '''polar circle''' of a [[triangle]] is the [[circle]] whose center is the triangle's [[orthocenter]] and whose squared radius is

<math display=block>\displaystyle \begin{align}
  r^2 & = \overline{HA} \times \overline{HD} = \overline{HB} \times \overline{HE} = \overline{HC} \times \overline{HF} \\[4pt]
  &= -4R^2 \cos A \cos B \cos C \\[4pt]
  &= 4R^2 - \frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{2}
\end{align}</math>

where 
:{{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, and {{mvar|C}} denote both the triangle's [[vertex (geometry)|vertices]] and the [[angle]] measures at those vertices; 
:{{mvar|H}} is the [[orthocenter]] (the intersection of the triangle's [[altitude (geometry)|altitudes]]);
:{{mvar|D}}, {{mvar|E}}, {{mvar|F}} are the feet of the altitudes from vertices {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, {{mvar|C}} respectively; 
:{{mvar|R}} is the triangle's [[circumradius]] (the radius of its [[circumscribed circle]]); 
:{{mvar|a}}, {{mvar|b}}, {{mvar|c}} are the lengths of the triangle's sides opposite vertices {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, {{mvar|C}} respectively.<ref name= Johnson>Johnson, Roger A., ''Advanced Euclidean Geometry'', Dover Publications, 2007 (orig. 1960).</ref>{{rp|p. 176}}

The first parts of the radius formula reflect the fact that the orthocenter divides the altitudes into segment pairs of equal products. The [[trigonometry|trigonometric]] formula for the radius shows that the polar circle has a real existence only if the triangle is [[obtuse triangle|obtuse]], so one of its angles is obtuse and hence has a negative [[cosine]].

==Properties==
[[File:Polar circle4.svg|thumb|upright=1.25|
{{legend-line|solid black|Reference triangle {{math|△''ABC''}} and its [[tangential triangle]]}}
{{legend-line|solid magenta|[[Circumcircle]] {{mvar|e}} of {{math|△''ABC''}} <br>(centered at circumcenter {{mvar|L}})}}
{{legend-line|solid lime|Circumcircle {{mvar|s}} of tangential triangle<br> (centered at {{mvar|K}})}}
{{legend-line|solid #4169E1|[[Nine-point circle]] {{mvar|t}} of {{math|△''ABC''}}<br> (centered at [[nine-point center]] {{mvar|M}})}}
{{legend-line|solid red|'''Polar circle''' {{mvar|d}} of {{math|△''ABC''}} <br>(centered at orthocenter {{mvar|H}})}}
The centers of these circles relating to {{math|△''ABC''}} are all collinear–they fall on the [[Euler line]].
]]

Any two polar circles of two triangles in an [[orthocentric system]] are [[orthogonal circles|orthogonal]].<ref name=Johnson/>{{rp|p. 177}}

The polar circles of the triangles of a [[complete quadrilateral]] form a [[coaxal circles|coaxal]] system.<ref name=Johnson/>{{rp|p. 179}}

The most important property of the polar circle is the triangle is self-polar; the [[Pole and polar|polar]] of each side/point is the opposite side/point.

A triangle's circumcircle, its [[nine-point circle]], its polar circle, and the circumcircle of its [[tangential triangle]] are coaxal.<ref name=AC>[[Nathan Altshiller Court|Altshiller-Court, Nathan]], ''College Geometry'', Dover Publications, 2007 (orig. 1952).</ref>{{rp|p. 241}}
